elements.quote: The objective of our study was to conduct a living systematic review and meta-­ analyses of studies reporting pregnancy and neonatal outcomes
elements.reason: Abstract explicitly identifies the report as a living systematic review and meta-analysis.

elements.quote: The objective of our study was to conduct a living systematic review and meta-­ analyses of studies reporting pregnancy and neonatal outcomes by comparing the pandemic and pre-­ pandemic periods.
elements.reason: Abstract states the main objective/review question explicitly.

elements.quote: included English language studies that compared outcomes between the COVID-­ 19 pandemic time period and the pre-­ pandemic time periods
elements.reason: Abstract states main inclusion criteria (English language, comparative pandemic vs pre-pandemic studies); exclusion criteria not explicitly stated but main criteria are given.

elements.quote: We searched PubMed and Embase databases, reference lists of articles published up until August 14, 2021
elements.reason: Abstract identifies information sources (PubMed, Embase, reference lists) and the last search date (August 14, 2021).

elements.quote: Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-­ Ottawa scale.
elements.reason: Abstract specifies the risk-of-bias assessment method.

elements.quote: We conducted random-­ effects meta-­ analysis using the inverse variance method.
elements.reason: Abstract specifies synthesis methods (random-effects meta-analysis, inverse variance).

elements.quote: Forty-­ five studies with low-­ to-­ moderate risk of bias, reporting on 1 843 665 pregnancies during the pandemic period and 23 564 552 pregnancies during the pre-­ pandemic period, were included.
elements.reason: Abstract reports number of studies and participants; study characteristics summarized via risk-of-bias level.

elements.quote: There was significant reduction in unadjusted estimates of PTB (35 studies, unadjusted odds ratio [uaOR] 0.95, 95% CI 0.92-­ 0.98)... There was no difference in the odds of stillbirth between the pandemic and pre-­ pandemic time periods (24 studies, uaOR 1.11, 95% CI 0.97-­ 1.26...)
elements.reason: Abstract reports main outcomes with number of studies and effect estimates for each.

elements.quote: unadjusted odds ratio [uaOR] 0.95, 95% CI 0.92-­ 0.98
elements.reason: Meta-analysis conducted; abstract reports summary estimates with confidence intervals.

elements.quote: There was significant reduction in unadjusted estimates of PTB... There was an increase in mean birthweight during the pandemic period compared with the pre-­ pandemic period
elements.reason: Abstract indicates direction of effect (reduction in PTB, increase in birthweight) relative to pre-pandemic comparison group.
The abstract does not summarize limitations of the included evidence (e.g., risk of bias, heterogeneity, imprecision); limitations appear only in the Discussion.

The retrieved abstract text (text_2) ends mid-sentence in Results; no interpretation or implications section is visible in the abstract evidence. The Conclusion section (text_20) is separate from the abstract, so interpretation in the abstract cannot be confirmed.
No funding statement appears in the abstract evidence.
Registration (PROSPERO CRD42021234036) is reported in the main text (text_7) but not in the abstract.

elements.quote: Conflicting reports of increases and decreases in rates of preterm birth (PTB) and stillbirth in the general population during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-­ 19) pandemic have surfaced.
elements.reason: The abstract/introduction notes conflicting evidence (an uncertainty), and the Key Message describes current knowledge of pandemic effects on PTB and stillbirth, but a fuller account of existing knowledge appears mainly in the Discussion rather than a dedicated Introduction rationale.

elements.quote: Further studies from countries with high prevalence are needed and this review will be updated periodically.
elements.reason: The need for further evidence and a periodically updated review is stated in the Key Message, and the objective of a living systematic review is given in the abstract, but the importance/need for the review is not fully elaborated in the Introduction.

elements.quote: Recently, Chmielewska 59 et al reported results from a system-­ atic review and meta-­ analyses including studies evaluating studies assessing population-­ level impact during the pandemic period published up to January 8, 2021.
elements.reason: A previous similar review (Chmielewska et al) is identified and cited, and differences from the current review explained, but only in the Discussion; this is not presented in the Introduction as the rationale for the current review.
This is a review of pandemic-related changes in pregnancy outcomes (etiology/prognosis-type question), not a review of intervention effects, so no mechanism of action is required.
No complex intervention or delivery context is evaluated; the review examines population-level associations, so a logic model is not applicable.

elements.quote: The objective of our study was to conduct a living systematic review and meta-­ analyses of studies reporting pregnancy and neonatal outcomes by comparing the pandemic and pre-­ pandemic periods.
elements.reason: The abstract's introduction explicitly states the review objective: a living systematic review and meta-analysis comparing pregnancy and neonatal outcomes between pandemic and pre-pandemic periods.

elements.quote: studies reporting pregnancy and neonatal outcomes by comparing the pandemic and pre-­ pandemic periods
elements.reason: The comparison (pandemic vs pre-pandemic) and outcomes (pregnancy and neonatal outcomes, e.g., PTB, stillbirth) are stated, but the population (P) is only implicitly defined (general population pregnancies) and no formal PICO framing is provided.

elements.quote: Studies were included if they compared pregnancy outcomes between the COVID-19 pandemic period and pre-pandemic time periods and reported on any of the outcomes of interest. We excluded studies that only reported outcomes of pregnant women with COVID-19.
elements.reason: Eligibility is specified: comparative design (pandemic vs pre-pandemic periods), any study design, required outcomes of interest, and exclusion of COVID-19-infected-only populations; setting/population scope is further described via study characteristics.

elements.quote: we searched PubMed and Embase databases... for studies published up to August 14, 2021... and included any type of study design published in the English language
elements.reason: Report characteristics are specified: publication date limit (up to August 14, 2021) and English-language restriction.

elements.quote: Full-text articles excluded, with reasons (n = 27): Awaiting assessment (n = 9); Different outcome (n = 5); Different study objective (n = 5); Non-comparative studies (n = 4); Outcome of maternal infection (n = 2); No outcome data (n = 1); Editorial (n = 1)
elements.reason: The PRISMA flow diagram (figure_6, chunk text_13) visually distinguishes exclusion for 'Different outcome' (outcome not measured) from 'No outcome data' (results not reported), satisfying this conditional element.

elements.quote: Post-hoc subgroup analyses were conducted for the two primary outcomes after dividing studies into single-center (or selected hospitals/centers in an area), regional (statewide or province-wide) or national in scope.
elements.reason: Synthesis groups are specified: meta-analyses of pandemic vs pre-pandemic comparisons by outcome, plus subgroup groupings by study scope (single-center, regional, national) and meta-regression by pre-pandemic duration, linked to the review's comparison of pandemic vs pre-pandemic periods.

elements.quote: As we were interested in overall pregnancy outcomes, we did not restrict studies based on plurality (including both singleton and multiple pregnancies).
elements.reason: Rationale for the notable restriction (excluding COVID-19-only studies and not restricting by plurality) is provided; the Discussion (text_19) further explains the review was designed to evaluate population-level pandemic impact, not maternal COVID-19 itself.
